title: Salt in the water: you are that
hookLine: a proud son comes home after twelve years of study, and his father hands him a cup of salt water
carry: tat tvam asi: you are that

lines: A FATHER, A SON, A CUP OF WATER.
cards: Ninety-seven days ago you started with one syllable, om. Seven Upanishads later, the block ends on the story many teachers use to sum up all of them: a father, a son, and a cup of salt water. The son is Shvetaketu.
He left home at twelve to study with a teacher and came back at twenty-four, having learned all the Vedas, and, the Chandogya says, very proud of it.

teach.b: His father, Uddalaka, asks him one question. Did you ask your teachers for the teaching by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, the unknown becomes known? Shvetaketu has no idea what he means.

So Uddalaka teaches him, lesson after lesson, through the Chandogya's sixth chapter. One evening he says: put this lump of salt in the water and come back in the morning. In the morning: bring me the salt.
Shvetaketu looks. It's gone. Sip from the top, says his father.
From the bottom? Salty. You can't see it, Uddalaka says, but it's here, all through.
In the same way, there is a finest essence, and this whole world has it as its self. That is the truth. That is the self.
And that, Shvetaketu, you are. Tat tvam asi.
Hindus count it among the four mahavakyas, the great sayings, and its teaching is the heart of the Upanishads: the self in you, the atman, is not a stranger to Brahman, the reality in everything.
And the schools read it differently.

Advaita hears one reality without a second. Vishishtadvaita hears a self that belongs to God the way a body belongs to its soul. Madhva's Dvaita reads the words another way, keeping the soul and God distinct.
All of them treasure it. Many Hindus explain the folded hands of namaste the same way: a bow to the divine in the other person, the coworker who annoys you and the stranger on the bus included.
Like the salt, it's in every sip.

how: Hindu traditions treat these Upanishads as the heart of the Vedanta: students chant and study them with a teacher, and the great sayings, such as tat tvam asi and prajnanam brahma, are taught as summaries of the whole.

o: the king who asked where the sleeping self goes
the student who waited a year to ask Pippalada
the sage who taught his son with salt in water

p: salt in the water: you are that
five sheaths, bliss at the center
the wheel, the swan, the highest devotion

s: tat tvam asi comes from the Chandogya Upanishad
Uddalaka teaches it to his son Shvetaketu, again and again, in chapter six, once with salt in water.
near its end, the Aitareya says 'consciousness is Brahman'
prajnanam brahma, one of the great sayings.
every school of Vedanta reads these Upanishads the same way
Advaita, Vishishtadvaita and Dvaita teachers all treasure them, and read them differently.

games.q: someone online says tat tvam asi means 'you're god, so nobody can tell you anything.' what was Uddalaka actually teaching his proud son?
o: that Shvetaketu was already perfect and needed no teacher.
that the finest essence, the self of all, is hidden in him like salt in water.
that salt water is holy and should be sipped every morning.
games.why: the salt was gone from sight and in every sip. the essence of everything is the self, and that, Shvetaketu, you are. it's the lesson that humbled a proud student, not one that puffs him up.

practice: Sit in the posture from four days ago and take seven breaths, one for each book: salt everywhere; not this, not this; inward, sheath by sheath, to joy; consciousness is Brahman; the breath itself; the river reaching the sea; devotion, in whatever form is yours.
Then let the rest of the sit be quiet, with three words underneath it: you are that.

wordCard.voice: Uddalaka, the sage who taught his son with salt dissolved in water. Ninety-eight sessions in seven of the principal Upanishads, from om at the Chandogya's opening to bhakti in the Shvetashvatara's last verse, carry his thread.

orig.note: Sanskrit tat tvam asi: that you are. Chandogya 6.8.7 and the verses after it.

carryVoice: Your line: tat tvam asi, you are that. Tomorrow, a new book begins, the Yoga Sutras, with one small word. Block A, done.

sources.ref: Chandogya Upanishad 6.1 (Shvetaketu returns at twenty-four, proud), 6.8.7–6.16 (tat tvam asi; salt in water at 6.13)
Aitareya Upanishad 1.3 (the door at the crown) and 3.3 (prajnanam brahma)
